items.stem: Which Redis data structure is the natural fit for a score-ranked leaderboard?

options.rationale: Correct: sorted sets keep members ordered by score, ideal for ranking.
A string cannot rank many members by score.
Lists preserve insertion order, not score order.
A hash maps fields to values but does not rank by score.

items.explanation: Correct: sorted sets keep members ordered by score, ideal for ranking.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about the cache-aside pattern with Redis are correct?

options.text: On a cache miss the application loads from the source and then populates Redis
options.rationale: Correct: cache-aside fills the cache lazily on a miss.

options.text: A TTL helps bound how long stale data can be served
options.rationale: Correct: an expiry limits the staleness window when the source changes.

options.text: Redis automatically detects source changes and refreshes the cache
options.rationale: Redis has no knowledge of the source; invalidation is the application's job.

options.text: Cache-aside guarantees the cache is always consistent with the source
options.rationale: There is always a window where cache and source can diverge.
Expiry is commonly used alongside cache-aside.

items.explanation: Correct: cache-aside fills the cache lazily on a miss.

items.stem: What is the main durability trade-off of RDB snapshots versus AOF in Redis?

options.text: RDB can lose writes since the last snapshot, while AOF logs each write for better durability
options.rationale: Correct: RDB persists point-in-time snapshots; AOF appends operations for finer-grained recovery.

options.text: AOF uses less disk and is always faster to load
options.rationale: AOF files are typically larger and can be slower to replay.

options.text: RDB keeps every single write with no loss
options.rationale: RDB only captures state as of the last snapshot.

items.explanation: Correct: RDB persists point-in-time snapshots; AOF appends operations for finer-grained recovery.
